posts.text: 👤 AI has been keeping America’s economy afloat - but what if the boom goes bust? AI investment has become a major engine of the US economy, accounting for an estimated 25% of GDP growth over the past year, according to Barclays. That means even a gradual cooling of the boom could drag the economy down, the WSJ estimates. ♦️ AI stocks drive much of the market rally. Stocks now account for 35% of household net worth, against 26% at the peak of the dot-com bubble . A crash could force consumers to cut spending - dragging down growth ♦️ data-center construction added around 0.5% to US GDP growth over the past year (Barclays), so a pullback in construction would rattle jobs and suppliers ♦️ the AI debt boom , which ramped up reliance on borrowing, could turn an AI downturn into a broader credit crunch. Potential data-center loan losses could hit $2 trillion within a few years (Columbia economist Stijn van Nieuwerburgh) ♦️ US federal debt has already exceeded 100% of GDP , compared with 35% before the 2008 financial crisis. Investor fears over US debt could keep borrowing costs high, leaving the US and the Treasury with less room to soften an economic downturn Economists disagree on whether an AI bust would resemble the dot-com recession or trigger something worse, noted the publication, yet the longer the AI spending spree lasts, the bigger the potential losses if the promised profits never materialize. 👍 Substack | Chat | @geopolitics_prime

Exclusive: US rules out troops, military bases in Ukraine under post-war security guarantees, falling short of Kyiv's expectations U.S. negotiators have privately ruled out sending troops or setting up military bases in post-war Ukraine as part of security guarantees, exposing a gap between Washington, Kyiv and European allies over what those guarantees should entail, people familiar with the talks told the Kyiv Independent. President Volodymyr Zelensky is concerned that guarantees without foreign troops would not provide Ukraine with credible protection against another Russian attack. He has told allies that he does not understand what the U.S. commitments would mean without troops or bases in the country, one person familiar with the matter s aid.
